2.1

Cell Structure and Function

Key Points

  • Nucleus: houses DNA, directs cell activity. Nucleolus (inside): rRNA synthesis + ribosome assembly.
  • Ribosomes: protein synthesis (free-floating or bound to rough ER).
  • Rough ER (has ribosomes): synthesizes proteins for secretion/membranes.
  • Smooth ER (no ribosomes): lipid synthesis, detoxification.
  • Golgi apparatus: modifies, sorts, packages proteins/lipids from the ER.
  • Lysosomes: hydrolytic enzymes — digest macromolecules & damaged organelles.
  • Mitochondria: aerobic respiration, main ATP source.
  • Chloroplasts (plants only): photosynthesis.
NucleusRibosomeERGolgiLysosomeMitochondria
A generalized eukaryotic (animal) cell.
2.2

Cell Size

Key Points

  • As a cell grows, volume increases faster than surface area → surface-area-to-volume (SA:V) ratio decreases.
  • Lower SA:V = harder to exchange nutrients, gases, and wastes efficiently → limits max practical cell size.
  • Microvilli increase effective surface area for absorption without increasing overall cell size.
Surface-area-to-volume ratioMicrovilli
Trap: SA:V decreases as cells get bigger — a very commonly reversed fact.
Larger cubes have proportionally less surface area per unit of volume.
2.3

Plasma Membranes

Key Points

  • Fluid mosaic model: flexible phospholipid bilayer embedded with a "mosaic" of proteins.
  • Integral proteins span the whole membrane; peripheral proteins attach to just one side.
  • Cholesterol (animal cells) buffers fluidity — prevents excess rigidity at low temps, excess fluidity at high temps.
  • Glycoproteins: carbohydrate chains for cell-to-cell recognition.
Fluid mosaic modelIntegral proteinPeripheral proteinCholesterol
The fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane.
2.4

Membrane Permeability

Key Points

  • Small nonpolar molecules (O₂, CO₂) cross the membrane freely.
  • Small polar molecules (water) cross slowly, or faster via channels.
  • Large or charged/polar molecules (glucose, ions) need a transport protein.
  • Membrane is described as selectively permeable.
Selectively permeableSimple diffusion
Which molecules cross freely vs. need a transport protein.
2.5

Membrane Transport

Key Points

  • Passive transport: moves DOWN the concentration gradient, no ATP.
  • Active transport: moves AGAINST the gradient, requires ATP (e.g., sodium-potassium pump).
Passive transportActive transportConcentration gradient
Passive transport needs no ATP; active transport requires it.
2.6

Facilitated Diffusion

Key Points

  • Still passive (no ATP) — but uses a protein to help cross.
  • Channel protein: forms an open pore for specific molecules/ions.
  • Carrier protein: binds the molecule and changes shape to shuttle it across.
Facilitated diffusionChannel proteinCarrier protein
Trap: Using a protein does NOT automatically mean active transport — facilitated diffusion is still passive since it moves down the gradient with no ATP.
Channel proteins form a pore; carrier proteins change shape.

2.7

Tonicity and Osmoregulation

Key Points

  • Osmosis: diffusion of water across a selectively permeable membrane.
  • Hypotonic solution: lower solute outside → water moves IN → cell swells/lyses.
  • Hypertonic solution: higher solute outside → water moves OUT → cell shrinks/crenates.
  • Isotonic solution: no net water movement.
OsmosisHypotonicHypertonicIsotonic
Trap: "Hypotonic/hypertonic" describe the solution relative to the cell — not a fixed property of the cell itself.
A cell's volume response in hypotonic, isotonic, and hypertonic solutions.
2.8

Mechanisms of Transport (Bulk)

Key Points

  • Endocytosis: membrane folds inward around material, forming a vesicle → brings material IN. (Phagocytosis = "cell eating" large particles.)
  • Exocytosis: internal vesicle fuses with the membrane → releases contents OUT.
  • Both require ATP — significant membrane remodeling is energetically costly.
EndocytosisExocytosisPhagocytosis
Endocytosis brings material in; exocytosis sends material out.
2.9–2.10

Cell Compartmentalization & Its Origins

Key Points

  • Compartmentalization: dividing the cell into separate membrane-bound regions lets incompatible reactions happen simultaneously.
  • Endomembrane system: nuclear envelope, ER, Golgi, lysosomes, and vesicles work together, moving material via vesicles.
  • Endosymbiotic theory: mitochondria & chloroplasts descended from engulfed free-living prokaryotes.
  • Evidence: their own circular DNA, their own prokaryote-like ribosomes, and a double membrane (consistent with engulfment).
Endomembrane systemVesicleEndosymbiotic theory
The endomembrane system: a secretory pathway.

⚠

Commonly Missed on the Exam

  • SA:V decreases as cells grow larger — not the other way around.
  • Facilitated diffusion is passive, even though it uses a protein — no ATP is spent.
  • Hypotonic/hypertonic describe the solution, relative to the cell — always double check which side you're comparing.
  • Endo/exocytosis need ATP even though they aren't "pump" active transport — bulk membrane remodeling costs energy.
  • Endosymbiotic evidence: circular DNA + own ribosomes + double membrane — know all three, not just one.
  • Cholesterol's role is to moderate fluidity in both directions (prevents too rigid AND too fluid), not just "add stability."
